brief.head: The last time
brief.text: Objects leave our lives one by one, un­no­ticed, Ajay Shah said. He sug­gests notic­ing, as it hap­pens, that this may be the last time[[x3]] you do some­thing. {077-C02}

brief.head: Cards, rebooted
brief.text: In the mod­ern world, Ajay Shah said, a vis­it­ing card should be a QR code of your con­tact file’s web ad­dress; Google Contacts polls it, so up­dates ar­rive au­to­mat­i­cally. {077-C14}

brief.head: No one-way journeys
brief.text: For most of his­tory, Ajay Shah said, a de­par­ture might be for­ever. Amit Varma read the old Hindu in­junc­tion against over­seas travel as elders’ fear the young would never re­turn. {077-C08}

brief.head: Zero, the hard digit
brief.text: Rotary di­alling meant you knew many num­bers by heart, Ajay Shah said. “Good an­swer, but not the full an­swer,” Amit Varma replied: zero took the most ef­fort to dial. {077-J16}

brief.head: Only in Calcutta
brief.text: Calcutta’s phones barely worked, Ajay Shah re­called. One woman picked up the re­ceiver, found her­self wired into two strangers’ con­ver­sa­tion, and heard them talk­ing about her. {077-S12}

thought.label: Thought for the day
thought.text: But we talk too much. You also need a lit­tle star­va­tion of con­nec­tion.

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah unpack a bag of lost objects
lead.head: The things that made us

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 77

body: Amit Varma ar­rived with a mas­sive bag. Ajay Shah, his voice al­most gone, wanted to know what it was for. “I have a new voice for you in my bag,” Varma said, then ad­mit­ted he was kid­ding.
The bag held ob­jects from his past. The idea, he said, came from a tweet that asked what had grad­u­ally dis­ap­peared over the last twenty years with­out any­one re­ally notic­ing.
Neither host wanted a nos­tal­gia feast. Varma said he was glad to live in this age, and that we have pro­gressed a lot. But some of what was lost, he ar­gued, is valu­able for more than nos­tal­gia.

Shah sup­plied the frame. “We shape our ob­jects and then our ob­jects shape us[[x1]] in ways that go far be­yond the sim­ple func­tion­al­ity,” he said. When an ob­ject goes, the cul­ture built around it goes too. {077-C01}
## Nothing else to do

Varma’s start­ing point was the writer Sara Rai, Munshi Premchand’s grand­daugh­ter, whose child­hood mem­o­ries, in an episode they recorded, sounded like a beau­ti­fully crafted work of fic­tion. He asked how she re­mem­bered so much.
Her an­swer, as he tells it: “We had noth­ing else to do. So we looked at things.” {077-S01}
In the 1970s and 1980s, Varma said, books, music and films were scarce. Time was not. “We had a lot of time,” he said, and he spent much of it day­dream­ing. {077-C03}
Now, he said, we are “scrolling, scrolling, swip­ing, swip­ing”, and look­ing closely has be­come an in­ten­tional ef­fort. He called it a lament about him­self, not a com­plaint about the young.
## Effort as a gift
Then the bag opened: two mix­tapes Varma made at nine­teen for the girl he would later marry, recorded in real time on a dou­ble deck. What mat­tered, he said, was the ef­fort and the in­ten­tion.
Shah agreed. By de­mand­ing ef­fort, at­ten­tion and focus, he said, “we har­nessed the CPU sec­onds of the mind into doing this and that cre­ated beauty”.
Handwritten let­ters worked the same way. “When you write, you’re not only ex­press­ing your­self, you are shap­ing your­self,” Varma said. {077-C05}
Shah drew the les­son for today: email can carry the same care, if we choose to write it that way.
## A bag of worlds
Varma’s tour took in his father’s locked cup­board of 1967 *Playboy* mag­a­zines, an empty diary from 1986, his late mother’s hand­writ­ten recipes and an MTV vis­it­ing card that read “Manic Beast”.
Some ob­jects car­ried whole so­cial worlds. The house­hold ad­dress book, Varma said, held ev­ery­one you knew, and re­minded you of them each time you opened it.
A trip to the STD booth, per­haps once a week, meant a call had to be worth it. The land­line was one phone for the whole house, in a fixed place.
Shah, who brought no ob­jects, brought mem­o­ries: a hos­tel with one pay­phone, a three-metre map of India on the fam­ily wall, and a fa­ther who started CMIE with an evening of in­land let­ters.
He closed with cash. Its anonymity and uni­ver­sal ac­cep­tance, he ar­gued, are things we no­tice only once they are gone. {077-C13}
Varma had the last word: “Cash is free­dom.”

second.label: Founding letters
second.head: Sacked, sealed, sent
second.deck: Ajay Shah on how his father started CMIE with an evening of letters

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on how CMIE began with inland letters

body: On 13 April 1976, Ajay Shah’s fa­ther came home and said he had been sacked. Asked what he would do, he said he would start a new or­gan­i­sa­tion, to be called CMIE[[x2]]. {077-S04}

That evening he wrote a pile of in­land let­ters to friends all over India. Each ex­plained what had hap­pened, de­scribed the ven­ture and asked for spe­cific help. “And that’s how CMIE got started,” Shah said.
The les­son he drew was for email. A mes­sage can be quick and dirty, or it can be an essay, he said: Gmail keeps drafts, so you can edit for days “and only then you punch send”. {077-C06}

quote.text: CMIE got started with hand­writ­ten in­land let­ters sent out to friends all over the coun­try

third.head: From animal to beast

pic.caption: Amit Varma on his MTV visiting cards

body: Amit Varma was never the cor­po­rate type, or the net­work­ing type. But at MTV, his third job, he was told he needed a vis­it­ing card, and asked for his des­ig­na­tion.
He was a writer there. “I said writer is too bor­ing,” Varma re­called. So he asked for “Creative Animal”, and got it. {077-S09}

A cou­ple of years later came a pro­mo­tion, a raise and a title along the lines of se­nior su­per­vis­ing some­thing. Asked what he wanted on his next card, Varma replied with a ques­tion. “So I said, What is a pro­mo­tion from cre­ative an­i­mal? So I got Manic Beast.”

Later, briefly in­de­pen­dent, he had cards printed that read “Amit Varma nov­el­ist and blog­ger”. {#novelist} As he never net­worked, the cards oth­ers handed him at con­fer­ences went into the rub­bish or lay around.

p2.deck: From mixtapes to cash, what the objects of the hosts’ past did to the people who used them

quote.text: When you sit down and you cu­rate the music you love and you want to share, you are in a sense also cu­rat­ing your­self.

box.title: The tweet behind the episode
box.text: Amit Varma filled a bag with ob­jects, some kept since child­hood, oth­ers found when he cleared out his late father’s house[[x4]]. The idea came from a tweet that asked what has grad­u­ally dis­ap­peared over the last twenty years with­out any­one re­ally notic­ing. {#tweet}

sections.label: Mixtapes
sections.head: Love, recorded in real time
sections.caption: mixtapes for the girl he married
body: Amit Varma pulled two cas­settes from his bag, a TDK and a Sony. He made them at nine­teen for the girl he was woo­ing, who was sev­en­teen and whom he later mar­ried. {#nineteen}

Making a mix­tape was painstak­ing. Music from abroad was hard to find. On a dou­ble deck, one tape played while an­other recorded, in real time, and you worked out how many min­utes of songs would fit on a side.

That ef­fort was his first point. Making a tape for some­one, Varma said, says both “this is who I am” and “I want you to like this”. He made them for friends too, but with the peo­ple he was woo­ing, he claimed a “hun­dred per­cent strike rate”. {077-J02}
## Curating your­self

The sec­ond point was about the maker. Choosing what to in­clude forces you to ask what you like, why you like it, and why you want to share it with this per­son. {077-S02} A Spotify playlist, he said, takes a minute to make, for some­one with a mil­lion other things to hear.
Ajay Shah, “a wee bit older”, had done all the same things. Effort and focus, he ar­gued, had shaped them in ways many peo­ple today don’t quite know. {077-C04}
~ His mod­ern sub­sti­tute: a care­ful email about a few songs, with links, telling the story of the music and your life around it.

quote.text: When you sit down and you cu­rate the music you love and you want to share, you are in a sense also cu­rat­ing your­self.

sections.label: Letters by hand
sections.head: Long hand, long thoughts
sections.caption: letters written by hand
body: Amit Varma could not find his old let­ters, but re­called two kinds: sheets sent off lov­ingly in en­velopes, and the blue in­land let­ters in which his mother wrote to him when he was away.

Neither, he said, was a two-liner. Sit down to write a let­ter and you feel you must make the ef­fort worth it, so you build a nar­ra­tive. His friend the nov­el­ist Chandrahas Choudhury still sends him emails like that.
## Writing to think

Varma tells his writ­ing stu­dents that writ­ing shapes the writer, and cites Joan Didion[[x6]]: “I don’t know what I think until I write it down.” {077-J20} Handwriting is slower and phys­i­cal, and Ajay Shah added that be­cause it re­sists edit­ing, more brain power goes into it.

Historians, Varma said, can go through the let­ters of Nehru and Patel. Of Nehru, what­ever the crit­i­cisms, he said: “The man wrote in long­hand.” {#nehru}[[x5]] He doubted today’s lead­ers wrote let­ters, and won­dered whether they were lesser peo­ple for it.

Shah ranked Nehru’s let­ters to his daugh­ter, which be­came *Glimpses of World History*, among the great in­tel­lec­tual cre­ations, along­side J.R.R. Tolkien’s let­ters to his chil­dren, which turned into *The Hobbit*. {077-R03}
~ In Class 8, Shah and his friend Manisha Purohit sat one desk apart and lived two build­ings apart in Bandra East. They wrote each other let­ters any­way. {077-S03}

quote.text: Just you’re liv­ing two build­ings away. But it’s a de­light to write and get those phys­i­cal pieces of paper

sections.label: The diary
sections.head: Chapter one, and then nothing
sections.caption: the diary he never filled
body: Amit Varma’s fa­ther, a gov­ern­ment ser­vant, re­ceived stacks of of­fi­cial di­aries every year. Knowing his son wanted to be a writer, he would hand them over and say, “Beta, likho”: son, write.

In the 1986 diary, at the age of twelve, Varma began a novel called *Tales of Saint Johns*. Part one, chap­ter one was ti­tled “Tantalising Tantrums”, “which at least al­lit­er­ates”. {077-J07} He wrote a cou­ple of chap­ters, in hand­writ­ing far neater than today’s, and then pretty much noth­ing.
“So I think of this as an empty diary,” he said, a lament for all the writ­ing he has not done. {077-S06}
## The priv­i­lege of paper

The diary also pointed to some­thing he had taken for granted. Getting good at writ­ing takes vol­ume, enough pages that some can be thrown away. In many fam­i­lies, a child had only the note­books bought for school. Simply hav­ing some­thing to write in, he said, was “a sign of great priv­i­lege”. {077-C09}
Scarcity cuts both ways, Varma added. A child whose fa­ther buys him his one diary will value every page. But the same scarcity can paral­yse, let­ting per­fec­tion be­come the enemy of pro­duc­tion.
~ Ajay Shah an­swered with a line from William Blake: “In what fur­nace was thy brain?” {077-J08}

quote.text: So I think of this as an empty diary, which is my lament for all the writ­ing that I haven’t done

sections.label: The address book
sections.head: Everyone you know, in one book
sections.caption: the household address book
body: The ad­dress book, Amit Varma re­called, lived in one place, on a par­tic­u­lar shelf or in the din­ing room. It was or­gan­ised al­pha­bet­i­cally and was still chaos, with num­bers at the back and front and pa­pers shoved in­side.
What it held, he said, was “Dunbar plus”: a phys­i­cal record of ev­ery­one you knew, with their phone num­bers. {077-C07}
## A tribe in a book

Dunbar’s num­ber, Varma ex­plained[[x7]], is the idea that our brains evolved in pre­his­toric times to re­mem­ber about 150 peo­ple, roughly the size of a tribe. {077-R08} Of those, about five are close friends, and a wider cir­cle goes up to about twenty. {#dunbar}

The book held all of them, plus the gro­cer, the elec­tri­cian and the plumber. Every time you picked it up, it re­minded you that there were peo­ple in­side. Today, he said, if we are not in­ten­tional about friend­ships, we lose touch with so many peo­ple.
He was not sug­gest­ing that any­one clut­ter a house with ad­dress books, only that a more con­crete sense of one’s uni­verse might help.
~ Ajay Shah re­mem­bered his sis­ter Sadna, who has very high stan­dards of being or­gan­ised, copy­ing the chaos into a new diary every few years. Within a year or two it was chaos again.

quote.text: This is a phys­i­cal man­i­fes­ta­tion of all the peo­ple you know in the world with their phone num­bers.

portraits.caption: Robin Dunbar
portraits.credit: Festival della Scienza from Genova, CC BY-SA 2.0

sections.label: STD booths
sections.head: One call a week, make it count
sections.caption: the yellow STD booths
body: Before mo­bile phones, Amit Varma re­called, col­lege stu­dents queued at night at yel­low STD booths, some­times three to­gether, to call home. It might be a once-a-week thing, so you felt you had to have some kind of con­ver­sa­tion.
The booth could also be a site of pos­tur­ing. A new boy from UP opened a call to his mother with “Pranam, Mataji”, and ev­ery­one at the booths turned to stare. {077-J15}
## Always on, rarely ur­gent

Ajay Shah called asyn­chro­nous mes­sag­ing “a very dif­fer­ent frame of mind com­pared to ei­ther noth­ing or syn­chro­nous”. {077-C10} With the bar at zero, he said, we send “did you take your meds today” mes­sages.
The booths them­selves van­ished. When mo­bile roam­ing ar­rived, Shah said, more than a mil­lion booths[[x8]] and their mil­lions of em­ploy­ees went out of busi­ness al­most overnight. {#booths}

The gloom about lost jobs is mostly mis­placed, he ar­gued, cit­ing Ila Patnaik’s news­pa­per col­umn on the booths’ demise. “Most of the time in India, job loss is not a prob­lem be­cause there is a cre­ative dy­namic mar­ket econ­omy and peo­ple move on,” he said. {077-C11}
~ At IIT Bombay, Shah’s whole hos­tel shared one pay­phone. For in­com­ing calls, the watch­man came shout­ing his room num­ber, “two six two”, until he ran down. {077-S13}

quote.text: the watch­man would come shout­ing two six two and then you would run down and pick up the phone.

sections.label: Cash
sections.head: Small change, big freedom
sections.caption: why cash is freedom
body: Ajay Shah closed the episode with cash. “You don’t know what you’ve got till it’s gone,” he said.

He asked lis­ten­ers to think of two things. One is the uni­ver­sal ac­cep­tance in­fra­struc­ture around cash: you can walk up to any es­tab­lish­ment in the world, put up cash, and they will take it. The other is its anonymity. “Cash is glo­ri­ous,” he said.
## The panop­ti­con

In what Shah called dystopian places like China, the in­fra­struc­ture for ac­cept­ing cash has bro­ken down[[x10]]. In a fully elec­tronic world, he said, you are fully trace­able, and you know you are in the panop­ti­con[[x9]].
It was a point Vitalik Buterin had made when the hosts were with him in Madras. There is, Shah said, “some­thing beau­ti­ful about being able to use cash”.
Shah’s ad­vice to lis­ten­ers was to use cash more. It is, he said, a so­cial re­spon­si­bil­ity. {077-C13}

~ Before cash, Shah had talked about land­lines: one shared phone for the house, in a fixed place, that might ring and ring with no­body to pick it up. Rigging up an ex­ten­sion cord, he re­called, made it pos­si­ble to talk in bed. {#extension}

quote.text: Gentle reader, use cash more. It’s your so­cial re­spon­si­bil­ity to use cash more.

We claim that by de­mand­ing ef­fort and at­ten­tion and focus, we har­nessed the CPU sec­onds of the mind into doing this and that cre­ated beauty and it shaped us in ways that many peo­ple in today’s world don’t quite know.

p3.title: Stories from the bag
p3.deck: Locked cupboards, urgent calls and a map the size of a wall

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a locked cupboard and what it held
stories.head: What the almirah hid
body: In Amit Varma’s child­hood home, every Godrej steel almi­rah was left un­locked ex­cept one. The almi­rah in his father’s study was al­ways kept locked.

“Obviously, if you’re a young boy, you want to know,” Varma said. Something he was not sup­posed to see was some­thing he had to see. He found where the keys were hid­den and, one day when his fa­ther was out, opened the cup­board.

Among video cas­settes, books and other ran­dom things were mag­a­zines: a bunch of *Playboy* and a bunch of *Mayfair*. Varma brought two of the *Playboy* is­sues, from May and November 1967, when his fa­ther was twenty-five or twenty-six. {#dad26}

He re­flected on how lit­tle men of that era knew. There was no *Debonair* yet, Bollywood of­fered skewed no­tions of ro­mance, and there was no in­ter­net. “But how are you fig­ur­ing out what the hell sex is?” he asked.

Then he turned the old joke about read­ing *Playboy* for the sto­ries around. “No, the thing is I ac­tu­ally did,” Varma said, be­cause the mag­a­zine had a great tra­di­tion of pub­lish­ing the world’s best writ­ers. {077-J04}

A col­lec­tion of *Playboy* sto­ries he bought around 1998 or 1999 is one of his trea­sured books. It is where he first read Haruki Murakami, whose *The Second Bakery Attack* came out in *Playboy*, along­side Updike, Cheever and Nabokov. {077-R06}
~ In the 1980s, he re­called, the two pres­ti­gious places to pub­lish a short story were *The New Yorker* and *Playboy*. Ajay Shah added the magazine’s in­ter­view with Larry Page and Sergey Brin.
stories.why: Scarcity changes what things are worth. One locked cup­board held enor­mous value when lit­tle else was avail­able, and the pages that car­ried erot­ica also car­ried great fic­tion and long-form jour­nal­ism. {077-S05}
stories.postscript: Ajay Shah first came across *Playboy* in his IIT hos­tel wing, where, he said, “it was com­mon prop­erty”. {077-J06}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on his father’s locked almirah

stories.kicker: Amit Varma retells a friend’s story of a long-distance call
stories.head: Thirty minutes of Michael Porter
body: Amit Varma’s friend Narendra Shenoy had an ar­ranged mar­riage with Sheila. Her twin sis­ter had been paired with a talk­a­tive man, a great con­ver­sa­tion­al­ist. Narendra, Varma said, was not, and felt a lot of pres­sure. Sheila once even asked him whether he had some­thing to talk about. {#sheila}
They were in dif­fer­ent cities while Narendra stud­ied for an MBA. One day he called Sheila, feel­ing the un­stated pres­sure to be in­ter­est­ing.
“So for half an hour he tells her about the busi­ness phi­los­o­phy of Michael Porter,” Varma said. {077-S10}
~ Varma told the story in a chap­ter on STD booths, where a rare call had to be worth the trip. “So this is what boys were like,” he said.
stories.why: When a call was rare, it felt like a per­for­mance that had to be filled. Young men often had no idea what to say, Varma sug­gested, and Narendra filled the si­lence with busi­ness strat­egy.
stories.postscript: The full story is in Narendra Shenoy’s episode of *The Seen and the Unseen*[[x11]].

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Narendra Shenoy’s half-hour call

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a signal he missed for years
stories.head: The call that wasn’t urgent
body: Amit Varma went from a boys’ school to ju­nior col­lege at Fergusson College[[x12]]. He did not know how to talk to girls, he said, and could not pick up sig­nals.

There was a girl he played bad­minton with. One day she rang the bell at his home, which as­ton­ished him, since they had only met at col­lege. She had a friend with her, and said she needed to make an ur­gent phone call. {#urgent} He let her in. She used the phone, and then she left.
It took Varma years, he said, to work out that this was “some kind of ex­pres­sion of in­ter­est”. {077-S11} Why else would any­one walk into a ran­dom person’s house to use the phone?
~ He has no idea where she is now, he said, and would not give her name.

quote.text: I have no idea where she is now, and I’m not gonna take her name.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the badminton partner’s urgent call

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a map that covered a wall
stories.head: India, three metres square
body: In Ajay Shah’s child­hood home, one wall, about three me­tres by three me­tres, was cov­ered by a map of India[[x13]]. His fa­ther had bought the map that the Survey of India sold[[x14]] as four sheets, im­pro­vised a wooden board of the cor­rect size and pasted the sheets to­gether. {#map}
After that, Shah said, it was “stan­dard op­er­at­ing pro­ce­dure”: when­ever a place name or a river came up, the chil­dren would scam­per up to the map and look. {077-S14} He misses it.
Shah has tried for years to build a wall-sized map of the Himalayas, with­out suc­cess. He be­lieves one German com­pany makes a good six-sheet set, and asked lis­ten­ers for leads.
~ Amit Varma in­voked Borges: “The only ac­cu­rate map of the Himalayas would have to be as big as the Himalayas.” {077-J18}
stories.why: A huge paper map on a wall made ge­og­ra­phy part of fam­ily life, some­thing ev­ery­one looked at to­gether. Shah ar­gued that paper maps give a strate­gic sense that Google Maps does not. {077-C12}
stories.postscript: Children today, Shah said, can nei­ther read a paper map nor fold one.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the three-metre map of India

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 77. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Jawaharlal Nehru (Keystone View Company/FPG, public domain); J. R. R. Tolkien (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Robin Dunbar (Festival della Scienza from Genova, CC BY-SA 2.0); Haruki Murakami (Ministerio Cultura y Patrimonio from Quito, Ecuador, public domain); Jorge Luis Borges (Grete Stern, public domain). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon and Apple.

shelf.title: Sara Rai Inhales Literature (Episode 255 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Sara Rai’s strik­ingly de­tailed child­hood mem­o­ries, and her ex­pla­na­tion that ‘we had noth­ing else to do, so we looked at things’, which in­spired Amit’s ar­gu­ment that un­filled time sharp­ens at­ten­tion.

shelf.title: Chandrahas Choudhury’s Country of Literature (Episode 288 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A liv­ing ex­am­ple that email can still carry long, nar­ra­tive, mem­ory-filled let­ters if the writer takes the trou­ble.

shelf.title: Glimpses of World History
shelf.creator: Jawaharlal Nehru
shelf.why: Nehru’s let­ters to his daugh­ter Indira, a his­tory of the world writ­ten from prison largely from mem­ory.

shelf.title: The Hobbit
shelf.creator: J.R.R. Tolkien
shelf.why: Another case of a per­son writ­ing to fam­ily and end­ing up with a book the world trea­sures.

shelf.title: Playboy Stories: The Best of Forty Years of Short Fiction
shelf.creator: Edited by Alice K. Turner
shelf.why: Evidence that Playboy pub­lished the world’s best short-story writ­ers.

shelf.title: The Second Bakery Attack
shelf.creator: Haruki Murakami
shelf.why: The ex­am­ple Amit names of the high-quality fic­tion Playboy car­ried.

shelf.title: Google Guys: The Playboy Interview
shelf.creator: Playboy (interview with Larry Page and Sergey Brin)
shelf.why: Shows that Playboy ran se­ri­ous long-form jour­nal­ism along­side its fic­tion.

shelf.title: How Many Friends Does One Person Need?
shelf.creator: Robin Dunbar
shelf.why: Dunbar’s find­ing that we can sus­tain only about 150 mean­ing­ful re­la­tion­ships, in tiers of roughly 5, 15, 50 and 150, with most of our emo­tional en­ergy going to the clos­est few.

shelf.title: Toddy Chicken recipe video
shelf.creator: Wah Chef
shelf.why: His per­sonal favourite in the flood of on­line cook­ing videos.

shelf.title: Narendra Shenoy and Mr Narendra Shenoy (Episode 250 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A con­ver­sa­tion with Amit’s friend Naren Shenoy, with a charm­ing ar­ranged-marriage story; Amit plans to re­search the caste and class roots of cui­sine with him.

shelf.title: Creative destruction (column on the demise of STD booths)
shelf.creator: Ila Patnaik
shelf.why: A clear real-world case of cre­ative de­struc­tion: an in­dus­try em­ploy­ing mil­lions dis­ap­peared, and India’s dy­namic mar­ket econ­omy ab­sorbed the peo­ple.

shelf.title: Maps Are Magic (Episode 44)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ fuller dis­cus­sion of maps, which also gives Ajay’s ex­am­ple of a gen­uine dig­i­tal pub­lic good, in con­trast to UPI and Aadhaar.

shelf.title: On Exactitude in Science
shelf.creator: Jorge Luis Borges
shelf.why: Borges’s one-paragraph para­ble of car­tog­ra­phers whose per­fectly ac­cu­rate map is as large as the em­pire and out of date the next mo­ment: no rep­re­sen­ta­tion can fully cap­ture re­al­ity.

shelf.title: Let It Be
shelf.creator: The Replacements
shelf.why: Amit calls it the best album named Let It Be, ahead of the Beatles.

shelf.title: Answering Machine
shelf.creator: The Replacements
shelf.why: A great song with an im­mor­tal line, ‘How do you say good­night to an an­swer­ing ma­chine?’, whose sad­ness is lost on peo­ple who never used one.

shelf.title: Vitalik Buterin Fights the Dragon-Tyrant (Episode 342 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: A three-way con­ver­sa­tion with Vitalik Buterin on pol­i­tics and iden­tity, the source of his in­sight that the core weak­ness of vot­ing sys­tems is how eas­ily peo­ple can be bribed, and of Ajay’s ar­gu­ment that cash’s anonymity pro­tects us from a sur­veil­lance so­ci­ety.

shelf.title: Life Lessons
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit and Ajay’s course on what they wish they had been taught at twenty: learn­ing how to learn, frame­works for think­ing, writ­ing, prob­a­bilis­tic in­tu­ition, eco­nom­ics, the his­tory of thought, per­sonal fi­nance (Ajay’s mod­ule is ‘legendary’) and health.

shelf.title: The tweet that inspired this episode
shelf.creator: @NoContextHumans
shelf.why: The ques­tion that set off the whole episode about lost ob­jects.

shelf.title: After the Gold Rush
shelf.creator: Neil Young
shelf.why: Included in the episode’s show notes.

laughs.text: Ajay ar­rives hoarse and asks why Amit has a bag. Amit replies: ‘I have a new voice for you in my bag, so in case your voice goes.’

Editor Nomsita was brows­ing a long Playboy ar­ti­cle on psy­che­delic drugs, and Ajay asks if she’s un­der­age for them. Amit: ‘Nobody no­body is un­der­age for psy­che­delic drugs. So I’ve never had any. I’m just say­ing ran­dom things.’
Ajay on first meet­ing Playboys in his IIT hos­tel: ‘I mean in the wing it was com­mon prop­erty.’
Amit’s twelve-year-old novel ‘Tales of Saint Johns’ opened with chap­ter one, ‘Tantalising Tantrums’, ‘which at least al­lit­er­ates.’
Ajay ad­mits he never read Biggles. Amit: ‘Shocking. Your ed­u­ca­tion is in­com­plete.’

Amit once filmed him­self shirt­less on a cam­corder in the late 80s to re­mem­ber how thin he was. He has the tape but no VHS player, and says he won’t trust any­one with that ‘pre­cious footage. So it will re­main lost for­ever.’
Ajay on Amit’s habit of buy­ing Filofaxes he never used: ‘Gentle reader, he was think­ing about pro­duc­tiv­ity all along.’ Amit: ‘I’m fail­ing at pro­duc­tiv­ity all along.’

At the col­lege STD booths, a new boy from UP opened his call with a for­mal ‘Pranam, Mataji’ (re­spect­ful greet­ings, Mother), and ‘everybody’s just look­ing at him say­ing, What the fuck hap­pened?’
Ajay rounds off Amit’s diary story with ‘In what fur­nace was thy brain?’, a line from William Blake’s ‘The Tyger’.

The shared child­hood read­ing of their gen­er­a­tion: Enid Blyton (The Mystery of Banshee Towers, the Five Find-Outers, the Secret Seven), the Hardy Boys by ‘Franklin W. Dixon’, which Amit re­calls was a syn­di­cate of writ­ers, Biggles, and Alfred Hitchcock and the Three Investigators. On screen there was Alfred Hitchcock Presents, a Televista TV on four legs, Doordarshan as the only chan­nel, and weekly Chitrahaar.
Joan Didion’s ‘I don’t know what I think until I write it down’, which Amit cites to argue that writ­ing shapes the writer.
The Playboy seg­ment also notes that in the 1980s the two pres­tige venues for short fic­tion were The New Yorker and Playboy, and that India had no Debonair yet in 1967.
